Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE2202 : Power Electronics { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I (7 Hours)
Introduction: Concept of power electronics, scope and applications, types of power converters, power semiconductor switches and their V-I characteristics Diodes, SCR, TRIAC, power MOSFET, IGBT. Thyristor ratings and protection, methods of SCR commutation, gate drive circuits, switching and conduction losses in a generic power semiconductor device.
Module 2 :

Module-II (7 Hours)
Phase-Controlled Rectifiers: Principles of single-phase fully-controlled converter with R, RL, and RLE load, Principles of single-phase half-controlled converter with RL and RLE load, Principles of three- phase fully-controlled converter operation with RLE load, Effect of load and source inductances, Single phase and Three phase dual converters
Module 3 :

Module-III (7 Hours)
DC-DC Converters: Introduction, Basic principles of step-down and step-up operation, chopper classification study of Buck, Boost and Buck-Boost regulators, Introduction to forward and fly back converters.
Module 4 :

Module-IV (7 Hours)
Inverters: Introduction, principle of operation, performance parameters, single phase bridge inverters with R, RL and RLC loads, 3-phase bridge inverters- 180 and 120 degrees mode of operation, Voltage control of single phase inverters –single pulse width modulation, multiple pulse width modulation, sinusoidal pulse width modulation.
Module 5 :

Module-V (7 Hours)
A.C. Voltage Controllers: Introduction, principle of operation of single phase voltage controllers for R,R-L & R-L-E loads and its applications

Course Objective

1 .

To study the characteristics and operation of the various semiconductor devices.
2 .

To analyze different Power Electronic Controlled Rectifiers.
3 .

To learn the practical application of the different type of DC-DC converters
4 .

To learn the practical application of the different type of Inverters

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of the course, students will be able to
To learn the fundamental concept of power electronic devises

2 .

To analyze the operation of the different power electronic converters with various loads

3 .

Design and analyze power converter circuits and learn to select suitable power electronic devices by assessing the requirements of application fields.

4 .

Identify the critical areas in application levels and derive typical alternative solutions, select suitable power converters to control Electrical Motors and other industry grade apparatus.

5 .

Recognize the role of power electronics converters play in the improvement of energy usage efficiency and the applications of power electronics in emerging areas.

6 .

The student will be equipped to take up advanced courses in Power Electronics and its application areas.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE6531 : Air Quality Management { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I 8 HOURS
Structure of atmosphere, chemical and photochemical reactions in the atmosphere. Ozone chemistry- formation and depletion of ozone layer, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur.
Module II 10 HOURS
Filters, gravitational, centrifugal – multiple type cyclones, prediction of collection efficiency, pressure drop, wet collectors, Electrostatic Precipitation theory-particle charging-particle collection –ESP design procedure. Absorption: principles, description of equipment-packed and plate columns, design and performance equations. Adsorption: principal adsorbents, equipment descriptions – PSA – adsorption cycle-solvent recovery system-continuous rotary bed-fluidized bed, Design and performance equations.
Module III 8 HOURS
Acid rain mechanism of formation and effects. Photochemical smog, and sulfurous smog. Green house effect/global warming, green house gases, effects. Absorption: principles, description of equipment-packed and plate columns, design and performance equations. Incinertion: hydrocarbon incinertion kinetis, equipment description, design and performance equations.
Module IV 8 HOURS
Control methods – Processes based control mechanisms – mineral products – asphaltic concrete, cement plants and glass manufacturing plants Thermal power plants, Petroleum refining and storage plants, Fertilizers, Pharmaceuticals and wood processing industry.
Module V 8 HOURS
Dispersion models and receptor models with their practical applications

Course Objective

1 .

To provide students with a scientific and technical background in air pollution monitoring, pollution control technologies and environmental management.
2 .

Perspective on the air pollution issues
3 .

Understanding of the nature and parameters of Indian air emission and ambient air quality Standards
4 .

To have an indepth knowledge of air quality models

Course Outcome

1 .

1) Concept of dispersion of air pollution in the atmosphere
2) Design of air pollution control equipments
3) Can evaluate air quality management and analyze the causes and effects of air pollution
4) To develop a broad overview understanding of the strategies, regulations and policies to manage air pollution.
5) To be able to perform air quality modelling

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE4304 : Pavement Materials { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I: Soils: Origin and classification, particle size distribution and grading, and key engineering properties such as Atterberg limits, compaction characteristics, strength (CBR/resilient modulus), subgrade suitability, performance through soil stabilization techniques, including mechanical and chemical methods for enhanced strength, and durability. [8 hours]
Module–II: Aggregates: Sources, production, grading, and blending to achieve desired gradation, aggregate properties such as strength, durability, shape, texture, and resistance to wear and polishing through standard tests, ensuring their suitability for use in bituminous and cement concrete mixes for improved load transfer, stability, and long-term pavement performance, [10 hours]
Module-III: Bituminous binders and mixes: physical and rheological properties, grading, and suitability for varying climatic and traffic conditions, testing methods for binders and mixes, types of bituminous mixes, and principles of mix design, performance characteristics such as stability, durability, rutting, fatigue, and moisture susceptibility for long-term pavement performance. [10 hours]
Module-IV: Materials for cement concrete and semi-rigid pavements: cement, aggregates, water, and admixtures, and their role in determining strength and durability, mix design principles for concrete and stabilized layers, along with evaluation of performance characteristics such as strength, stiffness, and durability, non-conventional and emerging pavement materials (e.g., industrial by-products, recycled materials, geosynthetics), highlighting their applications, benefits, and practical limitations in pavement engineering.. [8 hours]

Course Objective

1 .

To gain a comprehensive understanding of the physical and mechanical properties of various conventional and non-conventional pavement materials.
2 .

To develop the skills necessary to analyze how physical and mechanical properties influence performance and durability of pavement.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Gain knowledge physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of various pavement materials.
CO2: Demonstrate the ability to select appropriate pavement materials based on characterization using conventional and advanced methods.
CO3: Integrate knowledge of soil and aggregate properties into the application of Granular layers of pavement.
CO4: Apply the principles of mix design for both bituminous and cement concrete, utilizing appropriate methods.
CO5: Demonstrate the ability to assess the performance and sustainability of advanced and recycled materials in enhancing pavement stability and durability.

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE2302 : Linear Systems { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction to linear systems, modelling of different systems, Math Preliminaries-I: Vector Spaces, Bases, Coordinate Transformation, Invariant Subspaces, Inner product, Norms, Rank, Types of Matrices, Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors. (4 Hours)
Module 2 :

Representation of unitary Laplace transform and its properties, representation of different linear-time invariant (LTI) systems in s-domain, Example of SISO/SIMO/MISO/MIMO system. (4 Hours)
Module 3 :

State space representations of continuous-time systems: various canonical forms, different representations from state space to state space and transfer function to state space, state transition matrix, solutions to LTI/LTV systems. (10 Hours)
Module 4 :

Equilibrium Points, Linearization, Types of Linearization with Examples, Controllability, Observability, Stabilizability, and Reachability. (4 Hours)
Module 5 :

Discrete time system representation: sampling process, Mapping of s-plane to z-plane, ROC, Pulse transfer function, Stability analysis of discrete time systems, Jury stability test, Stability analysis using bi-linear transformation. (6 Hours)
Module 6 :

Discrete-time state space model, various canonical forms, state transition matrix, Solution to discrete state equation. (6 Hours)

Course Objective

1 .

To familiarize students with different types of LTI systems, their modelling, and their solution.
2 .

To familiarize students with different properties of LTI systems.

Course Outcome

1 .

Students will be able to find out the transfer function of any given system expressed in the form of differential equations.

2 .

Students will be able to represent a system in state space form and will be able to find the solution.
3 .

Students will be able to represent a continuous system in discrete form and evaluate its performance.
4 .

Students will be able to analyze properties of LTI systems in state space form.

5 .

Students will be able to convert linear systems from continuous time to discrete time.

6 .

Students will be able to use different mathematical tools, provided by MATLAB and Mathematica.

Essential Reading

1 .

Bernard Friedland, Control system design: An introduction to state-space methods, Dover publication. , 2nd Ed.

Supplementary Reading

1 .

K. Ogata, Modern control engineering, Prentice Hall , 6th Ed.

Journal and Conferences

7435.t: EE4201: Modelling and Control of Power Electronics Systems
7435.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : EE4201 : Modelling and Control of Power Electronics Systems { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-1 (1-6): Small-signal analysis of dc/dc and dc/ac converters, State space average modeling, Discrete-time modeling, Modeling of dc/dc converters operating in CCM and DCM, Transfer functions.
Module-2 (7-11)-: Overview of various closed-loop converters systems, Voltage-mode and current-mode control, Complex behavior of power electronics systems, Laboratory techniques for studying nonlinear behavior.
Module-3 (12-22): Discrete-time modeling or iterative maps, Fast and slow-scale instabilities, Smooth versus Nonsmooth bifurcations, Nonlinear behavior of free-running converters, Nonlinear phenomena in power converters.
Module-4 (21-28): An overview of nonlinear control, Practical design of conventional hysteresis/sliding mode control, Fixed-frequency PWM-based sliding mode control, Sliding sector control, Model predictive control and its applications.
Module-5 (29-36): Control of power inverters: Power Quality Control, Application of H-infinity control.

Course Objective

1 .

To introduce the basic theory of pulse-width modulations and their applications in power electronics system
2 .

To understand various methods of modelling techniques of power electronics circuits and systems
3 .

To familiarize students with the principle of nonlinear dynamics and their application in switched converters
4 .

To impart knowledge of different control concepts and their advancement in the field of power conversions

Course Outcome

1 .

After successfully completing the course students will be able to:
• Develop a good insight into the modeling and control of power electronic circuits and systems
• Apply the advanced analysis techniques with strong mathematical fundamentals
• Develop the ability to compare and contrast the strengths and weaknesses of various modeling and control concepts
• Gain skills to understand operational issues and limitations of practical converters in industrial applications
• Examine practical uses and limitations of nonlinear models to analyze power electronics systems in industrial applications

Essential Reading

1 .

John G. Kassakian, Martin F. Schlecht, George C. Verghese, Principles of Power Electronics, Addison-Wesley Series

19211.t: ME2204: CAD and CNC Programming Techniques
19211.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : ME2204 : CAD and CNC Programming Techniques { 2-0-0 / 2}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Introduction to CAD and Computer Graphics (6 hours)
Overview of CAD systems and their applications. CAD hardware: video display devices, input devices, and hard-copy devices. Principles of computer graphics: 2D geometric transformations: translation, rotation, scaling, reflection, and composite transformations, Homogeneous coordinates for transformation representation. Basics of 3D geometric modelling: 3D transformations: translation, rotation, scaling, reflection, and composite transformations, 3D projections: orthographic, axonometric, oblique, and perspective.
Module 2: Geometric Modelling for Design and Manufacturing (8 hours)
Introduction to geometric modelling and its importance in design and manufacturing, Solid modelling techniques: Wireframe modelling, Solid modelling, Comparison and applications. Curve representation: Introduction to curves, Parametric and geometric continuity conditions, Spline representation: cubic spline interpolation, natural cubic splines, and spline specifications, Bezier and B-spline curves, Applications of curve animation. Surface modelling: Quadric surfaces, super quadrics, Bezier surfaces, and B-spline surfaces.
Module 3: CNC Basics (4 hours)
Basics of numerical control (NC) and computer numerical control (CNC): Principles of CNC and coordinate systems, Motion control and interpolation, Advantages and limitations of CNC machines. CNC machine architecture: Feed drive systems, spindle drive systems, and auxiliary systems. Automatic tool changers and CNC system software organisation.
Module 4: CNC Programming and Applications (6 hours)
Introduction to NC and CNC programming techniques. Manual programming: Coordinate systems, axis nomenclature, and elements of NC programs, Programming examples using G-code and M-code. Computer-aided NC programming: General-purpose NC programming languages, APT language. CNC system control architecture: Sensors in CNC technology and overall control system. Electrical drives. Current trends in CNC machine tool technology.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide a fundamental understanding of CAD principles, including creating and manipulating 2D and 3D models.
2 .

To familiarise students with geometric modelling, curve representation, and CNC programming techniques.
3 .

To explore hardware and software components of CAD systems and CNC machine architecture.
4 .

To impart hands-on knowledge of CNC programming, machine tool control, and modern trends in CAD systems.

Course Outcome

1 .

At the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Understand and apply CAD principles to engineering design and manufacturing.
2. Perform 2D and 3D geometric transformations and modelling for design applications.
3. Understand CNC principles, architecture, and motion control.
4. Develop and execute CNC programs for machine tools.
5. Analyse and implement various CNC machine control systems and hardware components.
